127.title: Fasting explained, never assigned
127.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep vratas, vows that often include fasting, on particular weekdays, festivals or lunar days: some eat only fruit and milk, some one meal, some abstain from grains, and a few go without water; children, elders, the sick and pregnant women are commonly excused.

segments.voice: Yesterday, surya namaskar, the sun salutation. Your line was bow to the sun. Did you face the light this morning, even for one round? Day one hundred and twenty-seven.

A coworker turns down the office pizza on a Monday. Not a diet, she says, it's my Monday fast. Another friend eats only fruit for nine days every autumn. Someone's aunt goes all day without even water, and at moonrise, the whole family gathers on the roof to watch her break it. From the outside it can look strange, or even a little extreme. From the inside, the people doing it usually look calm, even happy. So what's going on? First, a promise: nobody here is going to tell you to fast. Today is about what a fast is for. Today: fasting explained, never assigned.
screen: `A MONDAY FAST, NINE DAYS OF FRUIT.` → `WHY DO PEOPLE CHOOSE THIS?` → `EXPLAINED, NEVER ASSIGNED.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is vrata, a vow. That's the first surprise: in Hindu practice, a fast is usually one kind of vow, not the other way round. A vrata is a promise made for a purpose, for a set time, often to a particular form of the divine. Mondays, for many, are for Shiva. Some fasts come with festivals, like the nine nights of Navaratri. On Karva Chauth, many married women in North India fast from sunrise until the moon comes up. And there are many ways to keep one. The strictest is without even water. Much more common is eating only fruit and milk, or one simple meal, or giving up grains, or a single food for the day. Another word for fasting is upavasa, which people explain as staying near: near the divine, near the intention. That's the point. So what does the vow-fast actually do? It turns hunger into a reminder. Every time your stomach speaks, you remember why you chose this. The hunger isn't punishment; it's a bell that keeps ringing all day. It trains the will: you find out you can say no to yourself, gently, and survive. And it almost always ends in sharing: many fasts are broken with prasad, with family, around a table. The tradition itself is careful here. Children, elders, the sick and pregnant women are commonly excused, and many people keep a light version. A fast that harms the body breaks yesterday's line about the temple. The key word is the one in your carry: chosen.
screen: `VRATA — A VOW, NOT JUST A FAST.` · `FRUIT, ONE MEAL, OR NO WATER.` · `UPAVASA: STAYING NEAR.` · `HUNGER BECOMES A BELL.`

segments.voice: No fasting required, and if food is complicated for you, leave food out of this completely. Sit, and choose one small thing to skip for the rest of today. It could be a snack, sugar in your tea, or something that isn't food at all: one hour of scrolling, one complaint. Make it small enough to keep. Now give it a purpose: who or what is it for? Hold that for a moment. When you notice the missing thing later, let it bring you back here. The bell holds the time.
Vrata. A vow: a promise kept for a purpose and a set time, often by fasting, where the hunger becomes a reminder. Today's word.
Your line: chosen hunger. Today, each time you miss the thing you skipped, say its purpose to yourself once. Day one hundred and twenty-seven.

128.title: Sattvic
128.hook: food that calms; not a diet, a lens
128.howItsDone: Many Hindus aim for sattvic meals, fresh, simple and often vegetarian, and some also avoid onion, garlic and alcohol, especially on festival days, fast days or in temple kitchens; practices differ widely by family and community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vrata, the vow. Your line was chosen hunger. When you missed the thing you skipped, did you remember what it was for? Day one hundred and twenty-eight.

Think about two meals. The first: a huge, greasy late-night order, eaten fast on the couch while a show plays and your phone buzzes. Afterward you feel heavy, a little foggy, and somehow still restless. The second: a simple bowl of something warm, rice, lentils, a few vegetables, eaten slowly at a table by a window. Afterward you feel steady. Clear. Like you could sit quietly for a while. You don't need a nutrition label to know the difference. Your body tells you. An old Hindu idea gives that difference a name. Today: sattvic.
screen: `A HEAVY, RUSHED MEAL.` → `A SIMPLE BOWL BY A WINDOW.` → `YOUR BODY KNOWS THE DIFFERENCE.`

segments.voice: Hindu philosophy describes everything in nature as woven from three qualities, the gunas. Sattva is clarity, balance, light. Rajas is energy, drive, restlessness. Tamas is heaviness, dullness, inertia. Everyone has all three, and every day moves through them. Sattvic means full of sattva. The Bhagavad Gita, in its seventeenth chapter, applies this to food. Food that the sattvic love, it says, increases life, strength, health and joy: it's fresh, wholesome, nourishing and pleasant. Food the rajasic crave is too bitter, too sour, too salty, too hot and burning, and brings pain and unease. And food dear to the tamasic is stale, tasteless, spoiled, or left over too long. In practice, many Hindus take sattvic food to mean fresh, simple, vegetarian meals, and some also avoid onion and garlic, which are often counted as stirring or dulling. Families and communities differ on the details, and plenty of Hindus eat meat. Here's why it's a lens, not a diet. The question isn't only what's on the plate. It's what the meal does to your mind. Food cooked in a rage, gulped in a hurry, eaten while arguing, is hard to call calm, however healthy it is. So sattvic is also a way of eating: fresh, at a steady pace, with some gratitude. You don't have to change your menu to try it. Just ask of any meal: will this leave me clearer, or cloudier?
screen: `THREE GUNAS: CLARITY, DRIVE, DULLNESS.` · `THE GITA'S THREE KINDS OF FOOD.` · `FRESH, SIMPLE, OFTEN VEGETARIAN.` · `NOT A DIET: A LENS.`

segments.voice: If you have a small bite of something near you, a piece of fruit, a nut, a sip of tea, take it now. If not, picture your next meal. Before you eat, look at it. Where did it come from? Then eat one bite slowly, much more slowly than usual. Notice the taste, the texture, the warmth. Put it down between bites. When you've finished, sit and notice how your body and mind feel. Clearer, heavier, the same? Just notice. The bell holds the time.
Sattvic. Full of sattva, clarity: food, and a way of eating, that leaves the mind calm and clear. Today's word.
Your line: eat quiet. Today, eat one meal without a screen, at your own steady pace, and notice how you feel afterward. Day one hundred and twenty-eight.

129.title: Prasad again
129.howItsDone: Hindus receive prasad, food that has been offered to the deity, with the right hand or both hands, often touching it to the forehead; it's never refused or thrown away, and pilgrims often carry temple prasad home to share with family and friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sattvic: food and a way of eating that leave the mind clear. Your line was eat quiet. Did you eat one meal without a screen? Day one hundred and twenty-nine.

Someone comes back from a pilgrimage and knocks on your door holding a small box. Inside is one sweet, maybe a little squashed from the journey. They've carried it across the country in a suitcase, just to give you a piece. It's not a souvenir. You can't buy it in a shop near you, and it wouldn't mean the same if you could. They hand it over with both hands, and people in the house touch it to their foreheads before eating it. You've met this word twice already. Once with Ganesha's modak, once with the laddus in the kitchen. Today, the third time: prasad again.
screen: `ONE SWEET, CARRIED ACROSS THE COUNTRY.` → `TOUCHED TO THE FOREHEAD.` → `THE THIRD TIME: PRASAD.`

segments.voice: Prasad comes from the Sanskrit prasada, and before it meant food, it meant grace: kindness shown from above, a gift nobody earned. It also means clearness, calm. The Bhagavad Gita uses the same word for the settled, bright state of mind in which, it says, sorrows fall away. So yesterday's sattvic calm and today's blessed sweet share a word. You already know the path the food takes. It's cooked with care, offered at the shrine as naivedya, and comes back as prasad. Some temples are famous for theirs, like the laddu of the Venkateswara temple at Tirupati, which pilgrims carry home by the box. The same customs travel with it everywhere. You receive it in the right hand, or both hands. You don't refuse it, even if you only take a crumb. And you don't throw it away: if you can't finish it, you share it. Now here's what's new today. If prasad is grace that comes back, then the kitchen is part of the shrine. Many families say the cook's state of mind goes into the food: cook angry, and the anger is in the dal. Cook with care, and that's in it too. That's why many people cook for the shrine quietly, bathed, without tasting. And it's why cooking for someone else, carefully, can itself be a kind of offering. You give the best of what you made. And like the grandmother's laddus, the sweet returns.
screen: `PRASADA: GRACE, AND CLEARNESS.` · `THE LADDU OF TIRUPATI.` · `NEVER REFUSED, NEVER WASTED.` · `THE KITCHEN IS PART OF THE SHRINE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one person you could cook for this week. It doesn't need to be fancy: toast, tea, a bowl of rice, a sandwich cut the way they like it. Picture them. What would make them feel cared for? Now picture yourself making it, slowly, with your full attention, maybe with a little quiet in the kitchen. See yourself handing it over with both hands. If you'd like, offer it first at your corner. Hold that picture, and choose a day. The bell holds the time.
Prasad again. Grace you can eat: food offered, returned and shared, and the care that goes into cooking it. Today's word.
Your line: the sweet returns. Cook one simple thing for one person this week, carefully, and hand it over with both hands. Day one hundred and twenty-nine.

130.title: Ekadashi
130.howItsDone: Many Hindus, especially devotees of Vishnu and Krishna, observe Ekadashi, the eleventh lunar day of each fortnight, by avoiding grains and beans or fasting, spending extra time in prayer or singing, and breaking the fast the next morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prasad again: grace you can eat. Your line was the sweet returns. Did you pick a person and a day to cook for? Day one hundred and thirty.

Look at the calendar hanging in many Hindu kitchens. Not the phone calendar: the paper one, often a free one from the local Indian grocery store, with a picture of a god at the top. Every day has extra writing in tiny print: the phase of the moon, festival names. And about twice a month, one day is marked, sometimes circled in pen. Grandma circled it. No rice in the house that day. Maybe no food until evening. Nobody made an announcement; everybody just knew. Yesterday was about food shared. Today, food set down on a schedule. Today: Ekadashi.
screen: `THE PAPER CALENDAR IN THE KITCHEN.` → `ONE DAY CIRCLED, TWICE A MONTH.` → `TODAY: EKADASHI.`

segments.voice: Ekadashi means the eleventh. Eka is one, dasha is ten: eleven. The Hindu calendar follows the moon, and each lunar month has two halves, called fortnights: the bright half, as the moon grows toward full, and the dark half, as it shrinks toward new. Each half has fifteen lunar days, and the eleventh day of each half is Ekadashi. So it comes about twice a month, roughly twenty-four times a year. And because it follows the moon, it lands on a different date on your wall calendar every time. Ekadashi is especially dear to devotees of Vishnu and Krishna. The Puranas tell a story about it: that Ekadashi was a power, pictured as a goddess, who came out of Vishnu to defeat a demon while he rested, and was given this day in return. How is it kept? It's the vrata from three days ago, on a rhythm. Many people avoid grains and beans for the day, eating fruit, milk, nuts, or foods made from certain flours instead. Some fast fully. A few keep one Ekadashi a year without even water. The fast is usually broken the next morning, often at a set time, and many spend the day with extra prayer, singing, or reading. Here's the gift of it. A one-off vow depends on remembering. A rhythm carries you. Twice a month, with the moon, the day comes around whether you're in the mood or not, and it becomes part of how a household breathes.
screen: `EKA + DASHA: THE ELEVENTH.` · `TWO HALVES OF EVERY LUNAR MONTH.` · `DEAR TO VISHNU; NO GRAINS.` · `A VOW REMEMBERED; A RHYTHM CARRIES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think back to the last time you noticed the moon. Was it a thin sliver, half, nearly full? If you don't remember, that's fine; most of us don't. Tonight, if the sky allows, you might look. Now think about your own rhythms, the ones that carry you without effort: Sunday calls, Friday dinners, a monthly visit. Notice how they hold you. If you'd like one more, the moon is always offering it. You don't need to fast. Just notice the calendar. The bell holds the time.
Ekadashi. The eleventh day of each half of the lunar month, twice a month, kept by many as a fast day for Vishnu. Today's word.
Your line: a rhythm. Today, look up when the next Ekadashi falls, or just look up at the moon tonight, and notice where it is in its month. Day one hundred and thirty.

131.title: Rest
131.hook: sleep as practice; the mantra at bedtime
131.howItsDone: Many Hindus end the day by saying a name of God or a short mantra before sleep, and the Mandukya Upanishad's teaching on waking, dreaming, deep sleep and the fourth state is often linked to the three sounds of Om and the silence after it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ekadashi, the eleventh day, twice a month. Your line was a rhythm. Did you find the moon, or the next Ekadashi? Day one hundred and thirty-one.

Look at this week. It started with the body as a temple: this is where you live. Then a bow to the sun. A vow, and chosen hunger. Sattvic food, eaten quiet. Prasad, the sweet that returns. And Ekadashi, a rhythm set by the moon. Six days of caring for the building. But the thing the body asks for most, every single night, is the thing most of us treat as a leftover. We sleep when we've finished scrolling. We sleep when we collapse. What if sleep weren't the end of the day's practice, but part of it? Today: rest.
screen: `A WEEK OF CARING FOR THE BUILDING.` → `SLEEP, TREATED AS A LEFTOVER.` → `TODAY: REST.`

segments.voice: One of the shortest Upanishads, the Mandukya, takes sleep very seriously. It describes three states everyone moves through every day. Waking, when you're turned outward to the world. Dreaming, when you're turned inward, making worlds of your own. And deep, dreamless sleep, when there's no wanting and no picture at all, and the text calls that state full of peace, even bliss. Then it points to a fourth, beyond all three, the steady awareness that is there through them all. And it maps them onto the sound you learned on day two. Om is really three sounds, A, U and M: waking, dreaming, deep sleep. And the silence after the M is the fourth. So every night, you move through Om without saying it. That changes what bedtime can be. Many Hindus fall asleep with a name or a mantra: Ram, or Krishna, or Om namah shivaya, said quietly until it fades. Some elders connect it to an idea in the Gita, that what a person remembers at the very end shapes where they go next, and they practice the idea small, every night: let the last thing in the mind be something good. And the Mandukya's quiet point is that deep sleep isn't nothing. It's rest so complete that even the self stops needing to hold itself up. You can't force it. You can only put things down so it can come. Rest isn't time off from the practice. It's the practice, lying down.
screen: `WAKING, DREAMING, DEEP SLEEP.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE AFTER.` · `A NAME AS THE LAST THING.` · `REST IS THE PRACTICE, LYING DOWN.`

segments.voice: Tonight, try this at bedtime; for now, try it where you are. Put your phone face down, out of reach. Let your body get heavy, the way it does just before sleep. Breathe in, and breathe out long and slow. Now, silently or in a whisper, if you'd like: Om. Feel the A open, the U round, the M hum, and then the silence. Twice more. If you have a name or mantra of your own, let it be the last thing. Then just rest in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Rest. Sleep as part of the practice: waking, dreaming and deep sleep, A, U and M, with a name as the last thing before the quiet. Today's word.
Your line: put it down. Tonight, put the phone down first, then let a name or Om be the last thing in your mind. That's the week. Tomorrow we walk into a temple. Day one hundred and thirty-one.

132.title: The temple, explained
132.howItsDone: Visitors to a Hindu temple remove their shoes at the entrance, often wash their hands and ring the bell, then approach the inner shrine to see and bow to the murti, visiting smaller shrines and receiving prasad; most people come and go at any time, with crowds at arti times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rest: A, U, M, and the quiet after. Your line was put it down. What was the last thing in your mind before you slept? Day one hundred and thirty-two.

You're standing outside a Hindu temple for the first time. Maybe it's a grand carved one, maybe a converted warehouse off the highway with a painted sign. People are going in and out, easy and relaxed. And you're frozen at the steps, full of questions. Do I need to be Hindu? What do I wear? Where do I go first? What if I do something wrong in front of everyone? For three weeks you've practiced at home: the shrine, the flame, the food. This week you step out of the house and into the big one. Today: the temple, explained.
screen: `FROZEN AT THE STEPS.` → `WHERE DO I GO FIRST?` → `A NEW WEEK: TEMPLE AND COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: The Hindi word is mandir, from the Sanskrit mandira: a dwelling, a house. That's the key. A temple is understood as a home where the divine lives, in the form of the murti, the sacred image, which has been ritually installed and is cared for every day: woken, bathed, dressed, fed, and put to rest at night. So you're not walking into an auditorium. You're visiting someone's house. That's why the first thing everybody does is take off their shoes. There's usually a rack by the door. Many people wash their hands, sometimes their feet. Then, often, they ring the bell hanging at the entrance: your ghanta, announcing that you've arrived. At the heart of the temple is the innermost shrine, called the garbhagriha, the womb-house: small, often dark, lit by lamps, with the main image inside. In many temples, only priests go in. Everyone else stands at the threshold, looks, and bows. Above it rises the tower, which you can often see from the street. Many temples have smaller shrines too, for other forms of the divine, and people visit them in turn. There's often no single service everyone arrives for: most people come and go when they like, though arti times draw a crowd. A few quiet customs: dress modestly, don't point your feet at the shrine when you sit, and ask before taking photos. Most temples welcome visitors of any background; a few famous ones admit only Hindus. And if you're unsure, do what a guest does anywhere. Shoes off, watch, and follow.
screen: `MANDIR — A DWELLING, A HOUSE.` · `THE MURTI, CARED FOR DAILY.` · `SHOES OFF, BELL, THRESHOLD.` · `THE GARBHAGRIHA: THE WOMB-HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and walk in, slowly, in your mind. You reach the steps. You bend down and take off your shoes, and feel the cool floor under your feet. Maybe you rinse your hands. You reach up and ring the bell, and listen to it fade. Now you walk forward, toward the lamplight. Ahead is a small, dim doorway, and inside it, the image, lit by flames. You stop at the threshold. If you'd like, you put your hands together. And you just stand there, a guest in the house. The bell holds the time.
Mandir. The Hindu temple: a dwelling, a house where the divine is cared for every day, and where you enter as a guest, shoes off. Today's word.
Your line: shoes off. Today, when you walk into your own home, take a breath at the door as you take your shoes off, and treat it as a place where someone lives. Day one hundred and thirty-two.

133.title: Darshan
133.howItsDone: Hindus go to temples for darshan, standing before the murti with folded hands to see the deity and be seen in return; many also speak of taking darshan of saints, sacred rivers and holy places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mandir, the temple as a house where someone lives. Your line was shoes off. Did you pause at your own door today? Day one hundred and thirty-three.

Ask a Hindu friend why they're going to the temple, and they may not say to pray. They may say, I'm going for darshan. People travel for days, stand in lines for hours at famous temples, all for a few seconds at the front. Then the line moves on, and they leave happy. From outside, it can look puzzling. You waited six hours for three seconds? But ask them what happened in those three seconds and they'll tell you: I saw. And I was seen. Yesterday you walked up to the threshold. Today, what happens there: darshan.
screen: `SIX HOURS IN LINE.` → `THREE SECONDS AT THE FRONT.` → `I SAW, AND I WAS SEEN.`

segments.voice: Darshan comes from the Sanskrit root drish, to see. It means seeing, a sight, a vision. But in a temple it means something specific: to stand in the presence of the divine and look, and to be looked at in return. That second half is the surprise. Darshan isn't only you looking at a statue. Many Hindus understand the murti as truly inhabited, and so the seeing goes both ways. That's why the eyes of the image matter so much. Look at many murtis and the eyes are large, bright, sometimes made of silver or painted wide open. In the rites that install a new image, the eyes are often among the last things opened, and after that, the image is said to see. Some temples draw a curtain across the shrine at certain times, and when it opens, the crowd leans forward: darshan! Hands come together. Some people say a name under their breath. Some just look. You can take darshan of more than an image, too. People speak of darshan of a holy person, a sacred river, a mountain. Wherever the holy is present, you can go to see it and be seen. One more thing a scholar might tell you. Darshan is also the word for Hindu philosophy's schools, the classical systems of thought. They're called darshanas, ways of seeing. So the same word covers a glance in a temple and a whole system of philosophy. In both, the point is to see clearly. Three seconds can be enough, if you actually look.
screen: `DARSHAN — FROM DRISH, TO SEE.` · `TO SEE, AND TO BE SEEN.` · `THE EYES ARE OPENED LAST.` · `DARSHANAS: WAYS OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Find an image that matters to you: the murti in your corner, a picture of a deity, a photo of a teacher or someone you love, or simply the sky out the window. Sit where you can see it. Let your gaze rest on it, softly, especially on the eyes if there are eyes. Don't analyze it. Just look, the way you'd look at someone you've missed. Then, for a moment, turn it around: what would it be like to be seen like this, fully, without judgment? Stay with both. The bell holds the time.
Darshan. Seeing: standing before the divine, a holy person or a holy place, to see and to be seen in return. Today's word.
Your line: see. Today, look at one person, really look, for a full moment, the way you'd take darshan, and let them see you back. Day one hundred and thirty-three.
